newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Labour rivals bury hatchet, prepare for power.
newsitem.headline: NZ Labour rivals bury hatchet, prepare for power.

text.p: Former Labour leader Mike Moore scotched rumours of continued acrimony between him and leader Helen Clark by campaigning in public with her for the first time on Thursday.

On Thursday the two campaigned together in the Wellington Labour stronghold of Mana and afterwards jointly gave an impromptu press conference at which they outlined their plans for negotiating to form a government after the October 12 election.

Clark said Moore would be part of a negotiating team including herself, finance spokesman Michael Cullen, Labour president Michael Hirschfeld and possibly others which would negotiate with other parties and produce "a document showing what this government is about".
Moore moved a vote of thanks to Clark after her public speech. Later Clark told journalists the two had always planned to meet "somewhere on the trail" and they were both in Wellington today.

Moore said looking at the crowd's faces "there was a sigh of relief" that Labour had "a dedicated person to the removal of the Bolger-Birch government and more importantly stop any hope there might be a Prebble-led National government".

Jim Bolger is the ruling conservative National Party Prime Minister and Bill Birch is his Finance Minister. Richard Prebble is the leader of the free-market Act New Zealand which is likely to support a National government.
"If that doesn't motivate your basic instincts and principles nothing will," Moore said.
Moore declined to criticise Labour's potential ally, left wing Alliance leader Jim Anderton.
He said he would prepare papers on how policies could be negotiated and be fully briefed for talks after the election.

"There will be an anti-National government. At the last election 66 percent did not want this government. It would be an appalling situation and a shame on all of us - Mr Anderton, Helen Clark or (New Zealand First leader) Winston Peters if at the end because of our own egos and ambitions we let New Zealand down by allowing Mr Bolger to continue," Moore said.

He said Bolger, who has said New Zealand is an Asian nation, should explain how he would form a government with the backing of the Christian Coalition "who have contempt for the faith of most nations in our region" and how he could go to Indonesia and explain how he was in power "on the back of those who think the Moslem God is inferior to their own".
Clark deposed Moore in 1993 after Labour narrowly lost the election to the ruling conservative National Party.
Only two weeks ago Moore finally accepted her long-standing invitation to return to the front bench and accepted the spokesmanship of trade and foreign affairs.
But when Clark visited Moore's hometown of Christchurch on Tuesday the two did not meet, fuelling speculation that the reconciliation was not complete.
